verified.band_edge_check:
I agree that the sides should be softened. I disagree with the reason that the edge is 'too hard for a real snoot'.

Reproduced: E's toe is 29-32 px on the left and 33-45 px on the right, against D's 53-69 px. That is 5.7-8.8 mm at 0.195 mm/px. The 50 % lines move only 14-15 px over the base's height. The steepest step at 480 is 0.32 / 0.35 L* per px, against D's 0.25 / 0.23. The numbers show no dip outside either edge. At 100 % and at 2x I see a panel with defined sides, the left sharper. At 480 1x I see a lighter centre with a visible left edge.

Physics:
- Throw. The pool's 50 % half-width is 39.6 mm, which puts a 12 degree cone about 0.39-0.44 m away.
- A real tube snoot on a 3 mm emitter. Its penumbra is 3 mm x (410 - L) / L for a tube of length L: 21.6 mm for a 50 mm tube, 9.3 mm for 100 mm, 5.2 mm for 150 mm. The 10-50 % part is about 0.35 of that: 7.5 / 3.2 / 1.8 mm. So E's 5.7-8.8 mm toe equals a tube about 45-65 mm long, and any longer tube cuts harder. Real snoots on small LEDs cut this hard or harder.
- The base itself. E's toe has a Gaussian-like foot that a bare Cycles cone does not make. A crude fit (fit_out.txt) models it as the spot's cone edge times the cone surface's falloff, blurred by a Gaussian. It gives E a blend of about 0.15-0.35 with about 6 mm of extra spread, and D a blend of about 0.35 with 8 mm or more. That extra spread is probably light travelling sideways in the acrylic over the liner, which is part of what a satin cone does.
- So E is physically possible, at the hard end. It is not beyond what a real light gives.

Why soften anyway:
1. The owner's rule that a snoot cuts soft, and the painted-panel look at 100 % and 2x. He looks at the base closely.
2. Coherence with the flag. In a real rig the flag sits beyond the snoot's mouth, so it cuts at least as hard as the mouth. In E the flag's cut is far softer than the sides: the foot keeps about 73 % of the pool, and the floor just in front still gets 12.6-13.6 against D's 17.8-18.3. That is the reverse of a real rig. Sides at least as soft as the flag would make the rig consistent.

The lever:
- I agree it is the spot's blend. The Cycles code confirms the critic. light_spot.h lines 104 and 140 apply the cone attenuation along the direction from each sampled point on the source. scene_light.cpp line 1373 sets spot_smooth = 1 / ((1 - cos half) x blend). lights.py builds a plain Blender SPOT with no tube modelled. A 1.5 mm radius at 0.41 m adds only about 0.21 degrees.
- D's softer edge most likely came from D's larger source: the same fit gives D about the same blend but more blur. So the coordinator is right about what changed from D to E, and the critic is right about what sets E's edge now.
- I agree to keep the 3 mm source, the flag, #FFF4E8, 7.5 W and the aim. The pool is centred at x 819-820 against the base axis at 821. A larger source would also soften the flag's cut and bring floor spill back.

What I would add:
- A higher blend only lowers the light, so the floor cannot get worse.
- It does pull the 50 % line inward: about 5.5 degrees falls to about 4.65 degrees at blend 0.8, roughly 30 px narrower per side. It also lowers the base median a little. Re-check the band width and the base's 47/1/1, and widen the cone 1-2 degrees if the band gets too narrow.
- The critic's target (toe of 55-65 px or more, no more than 0.25 L* per px at 480) is sensible, since D already met it.
verified.base_check:
I agree with the critic's order: LIT-e with softer sides first, LIT-e as it is second, LIT-c last, and LIT-d out.

Why, from my own numbers:
- Base. E's base reads as the deep red pour at page size: median 47/1/1, L* 5.7, C* 24.2, centre band L* 6.3-8.2. C's base is 22/0/0, L* 1.5, C* 7.3, with 97 % of it below L* 2.5 at 480. On the 480 sheet it reads as a black base under a red ball, right after OFF.
- Plum. It is gone. E's stripe is 52.5/4.7/3.7 (G above B, h 24.1 against the side's 21.5). D's stripe was 51.5/4.5/8.6.
- Floor. D's column peaked at L* 21.3. E is 17.0-17.7 across x 640-920 against 15.5 and 16.5 beside it: a broad lift of 1-2 L*. It is red (the added light's G/R is 0.28, against about 0.81 for house white on this floor), so it is mostly bounce from the lit base, which is physically expected. I could not see it at normal exposure at 480 or at 100 %, only at +2 stops.
- No new faults. Comparing E with C and D, there are only isolated noise pixels on the ball and noise in the lip glow. Nothing new shows in v_lip2x_cde.png.
- Glow. The lite_out figures (41.8/86.6/40.0 against C's 42.0/86.9/40.0) show it unchanged. I did not rerun the glow mask myself.

One correction for how this goes to the owner: LIT-e as it stands is honest and physically possible. A short tube snoot on a 3 mm LED gives this edge. The reasons to soften are his soft-cut rule, the panel look at 100 % and 2x, and matching the flag's softer cut. The physics does not call the current edge impossible.

The fix is a higher blend alone. Since a higher blend only lowers the light, re-check the base median and the band's width as well as the floor.

If there is no re-render, LIT-e as it is still beats LIT-c: E's fault shows only at 100 % and 2x, while C's base reads black at page size.

found.band_edge: As rendered, the edge is too hard. At full size, each side of the band rises about 3 L* (1.9 to 5.0 on the left) within roughly 45 px, then hits a shoulder. The steepest slope is 0.9 L* per 10 px, against D's 0.5. The 20-80 % width is about 55-70 px, against D's 70-85. Mach bands at the foot and shoulder turn this into two parallel vertical lines, and the left one looks harder because its shoulder is abrupt while the right edge has a gentle lead-in. At 100 % and on a 2x screen it reads as a painted panel or a two-tone base. At 480 1:1 it reads as a soft lighter centre with a visible left edge. Is it what a real rig gives? It is the light, not the model: OFF's base is smooth there, and the edges bow outward 15-20 px as a round pool's sides should. By my estimate, a 12-degree pool about 82 mm wide puts the snoot mouth about 0.4 m away. A 3 mm emitter in a tube snoot would then cast a penumbra of roughly 8-15 mm, or 40-75 px. So E's edge is honest but at the hard end, and no product photographer would leave it there; it also breaks the owner's 'cuts soft'. The fix is a softer cone edge: a grid or a softer-edged spot, or D's source size if the flag still keeps the floor at or below about 18 L*. Aim for about 110-130 px per side (10-90 %), keep the half-light points near x 612 and x 1028, and keep the colour, the flag and the power. My blur mock-ups (not renders) read as a natural pool at sigma 40 px, and at sigma 20 px with only a faint left edge. A different aim will not remove the edges, because they are the pool's own left and right sides. A wider cone would push them off the base, but it would also send spot light onto the polished ball and the floor beside the base; I have not tested that.

verdicts.reasoning: The fault is real and sits where the critic says. At 100 % and at 960 (480 CSS px on a 2x screen), E's base shows a lighter maroon panel between two defined vertical lines, the left one crisper. D's sides fade more gradually. At 480 1:1 both edges are visible: the left one near x180, clearer, the right one fainter. The centre reads as a lighter band. It is the light, not the mesh: OFF's base is smooth there. Two corrections to the evidence. (1) The 20-80 % widths depend on which level is taken as 100 % and should not be quoted. The robust difference is the edge's foot: E's steepest slope is 1.6-1.8 times D's, and its 10-50 % rise is about 40 px against about 68. The critic's proposed target of 110-130 px (10-90 %) is already met by E as it stands (their own script gives 99-147 px), so it cannot steer a re-render. (2) The pool's sides are nearly straight: the half-width stays 182-194 px from the lip to the bottom. That is not 'as a round pool's sides should' bow. Take about 4.8 px/mm (the base's 150 mm is 723 px in OFF), a face about 52-55 mm tall (y about 1515-1781) and a half-width of about 39 mm at mid-face. A round pool of that size would narrow to about 29 mm (about 145 px) at the lip and at the bottom, a bow of 40-50 px per side. E's sides bow 7-19 px. The parallel straight sides add to the painted-panel read. Severity is fix, not blocking: at 480 1x it still reads as light. But on a 2x screen at page size the two-tone panel shows, and this owner studies the base, so it must be fixed before he sees it.

verified.band_edge_check:
I agree with the diagnosis and the cure, but not with the reasoning about the pool's shape or with the target.

What reproduces: the edge comes from the light, since OFF's base is smooth there. The left side climbs about 3 L* in about 45 px to a shoulder at x632-640. The slope is 0.89-0.91 L* per 10 px against D's 0.50-0.56. At 100 % and at 960 it reads as a two-tone panel; at 480 1:1 it reads as a lighter centre with both edges visible, the left one clearer. I also agree that re-aiming cannot remove side edges and that softening is the fix.

I measured the critic's blur mock-ups, which are not renders. Sigma 40 reads as a natural pool and gives a slope of 0.40-0.45 with a 10-50 % rise of 78-84 px. Sigma 20 gives 0.55-0.62 and 53-56 px, about the same as D (0.50-0.56, 66-70 px). The spec should therefore be: steepest slope at most about 0.45 L* per 10 px, and a 10-50 % rise of at least about 80 px. Measure on rows 1580-1700, using the added light over LIT-c, with the band's centre (median x760-880) as the 100 % reference. The critic's '110-130 px 10-90 %' does not work as a spec, because E already meets it.

Physics: at about 4.8-5.1 px/mm, the half-light width of about 380 px (75-80 mm) puts a 12-degree apex about 0.37-0.39 m away. D's floor footprint, narrowing from about 350 to 265 px over about 100 mm of floor, agrees. A 3 mm emitter at the back of an 80-150 mm tube snoot casts a full penumbra of source x distance / tube length = 8-15 mm (40-75 px). Only about 15-25 px of that lies between the 10 % and 50 % points. E's 38-41 px is therefore no harder than that rig would really cast, if anything slightly softer. So the physics is honest and the hardness is a stylistic choice a product photographer would avoid. The case for softening is the look and the owner's 'cuts soft' rule, not a physics fault. A grid, a larger source or diffusion is the real-studio way to do it.

Where I disagree: 'the edges bow 15-20 px as a round pool's sides should' is wrong. A round pool this wide on a face about 52-55 mm tall would bow 40-50 px per side. E's sides bow 7-19 px (left x623-639, right x1000-1017, from y1520 to y1780). The added-light map shows a near-rectangle, as if the beam were a vertical slot or an ellipse at least 2.3:1 tall. So the light's real shape (spot object scale, area-light shape, snoot geometry) should be checked when the edge is softened: a round snoot or grid should give sides that visibly curve in toward the lip and the bottom.

I also agree that a much wider cone is risky, and the risk is sharper than the critic says. The polished ball's glint point for a light low in front sits near the middle of the ball's front, about 16-18 degrees off the beam axis. Any cone wider than about 30 degrees would put the spot's reflection there.
